A whole computer, built from familiar ideas

PROCESSOR · MEMORY · INPUT / OUTPUT

From a binary number to a logic gate, from a full adder to a register, and from stored instructions to a processor: the computer on your desk brings those ideas together.

Explore its processor, memory, and input/output. Change a value, follow a signal, and see how bits can represent an instruction, a key report, a color, or a sound sample.

Digital information, physical hardware

Voltage, charge, light, sound, heat, and motion are physical quantities. Circuits assign meaning to signal levels, store information in physical states, and convert between digital representations and the world around us.

How to explore

  • Drag the 3D model to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.
  • Click a component or its label. Use Browse for a complete component list.
  • Open the tower for the motherboard, processor, memory, and controllers. Use Return to desktop to return to the external devices.
  • Drag the divider between the 3D scene and the experiment to change their widths. Double-click the divider to reset it. Scroll over an image or audio waveform to zoom. Drag an image to pan, or drag an audio waveform to move its sample cursor.
  • Use Follow a keystroke beside the tower button for a six-stop system story.
  • The building blocks below the model highlight ideas used by the selected component. Select I/O interfaces to connect device signals to values that software reads and writes.

About the models

The desktop and chip diagrams are schematic. They show roles and relationships without reproducing a particular product. USB waveforms follow the selected protocol rules; thermal, timing, and memory-decay animations use simplified values to make their behavior visible. Model notes inside each experiment explain the relevant assumptions.

Conceptualized by Adelson Chua, EEEI, University of the Philippines Diliman.

Digital building blocks, working together

A complete computer combines these ideas at many scales.

Building blockWhere it appears
Number representationRGB channels, instruction bytes, key reports, signed audio samples, and mouse displacement.
Gates and Boolean logicArithmetic units, bit tests, instruction decoding, and control decisions.
Binary arithmeticCPU calculations, address computation, GPU shading, and sample processing.
Multiplexers and decodersSelecting operands, choosing a destination, decoding an instruction, and addressing stored words.
Flip-flops and registersPreserving processor state, sequencing instructions, and buffering transfers. DRAM and flash use different physical storage cells.
Instruction sets and datapathsMachine instructions select operations in connected circuits. Different architectures encode instructions differently.
Hardware and softwareMachine instructions give software a way to control the processor. Assemblers and compilers translate programs into those instructions.
I/O interfacesPrograms read input values, test status bits, and write output values. Keyboard and mouse reports, display pixels, audio samples, and storage transfers pass through device interfaces and controllers.

Sources & model notes

Embedded photograph and recording

  • NASA: Apollo 17 Blue Marble photograph. The original 1972 astronaut photograph is resized to 384 × 216 RGB pixels for this explorer; it is not the later satellite mosaic.
  • NASA/JPL-Caltech: Apollo 11 recorded speech. The Earth-version recording is used, downmixed to mono and resampled to 16 kHz. The Mars-altered version is not used.

Technical references

  • Intel instruction and architecture manuals · AMD64 architecture manuals · Apple Arm64 documentation
  • USB 2.0 specification · HID specification and boot reports · USB-IF CRC examples
  • NVIDIA GPU computing · AMD RDNA architecture · Intel Xe architecture
  • Samsung: DRAM · KIOXIA: NAND flash storage
  • CORSAIR: example ATX voltage rails · Intel: processor temperature and thermal protection
  • Analog Devices: analog-to-digital conversion

What the models represent

  • Display: 24-bit RGB values from the embedded image, with nearest-neighbor enlargement. Active-image throughput excludes link overhead, blanking, and compression. Enlarged pixels use a schematic RGB stripe layout; actual panel layouts vary. A separate slowed scan animation shows sequential updates while the timing readouts use the chosen resolution and refresh rate.
  • Audio: a sine wave or actual recording. Sampling and quantization views operate on those source samples. A drawn connecting line is a visual reference; it does not recover the original continuous microphone voltage. No microphone permission or live recording is used.
  • USB: a constructed full-speed IN/DATA0/ACK example with CRCs, bit stuffing, NRZI, and D+/D− line states. Keyboard capture translates browser key events into representative HID reports; it does not read raw USB traffic. It is a protocol illustration, not an electrical compliance test.
  • CPU: real example instruction encodings with conceptual execution steps. Core diagrams and timing are schematic, not a particular chip layout or performance claim.
  • GPU: parallel tile batches illustrate graphics work. GPUs also perform general-purpose computing and are processors in their own right. The explorer groups graphics with I/O to emphasize its display role.
  • Memory: charge storage, refresh, and retention are simplified and greatly slowed. RAM after loss of retention is shown as unknown; flash retention is shown over this short experiment, not as a promise of permanent storage.
  • Power and cooling: illustrative loads, energy balance, and thermal response. Controls change only this model. Actual specifications and thermal limits depend on the hardware.

Single-file implementation

All runtime code, geometry, media, and styles are embedded. The explorer works offline; reference links require a connection. Three.js is used under the MIT license included in this file. A software renderer provides a fallback when WebGL is unavailable.
